title: what the Rig Veda is
hook: a man swears off the slot machines, then hears the jingle from the next room. The Rig Veda keeps a gambler's own confession
tomorrow: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")

segments.voice: Yesterday, what the Rig Veda is: Ushas, the dawn, seen by those before us, by us, and by those still to come. Did you catch the first light this morning before a screen? Day one thousand two hundred forty-nine.

He promised. He meant it. No more, not this time. He walks past the casino floor toward the exit, keys in his hand, proud of himself. And then, from somewhere behind a row of machines, comes the sound: the bright little jingle of someone winning. His feet slow down. His hand goes to his pocket. The promise was real, and so is the pull, and the pull is winning. Anyone who has tried to quit anything, a habit, a phone, a drink, may know the shape of that moment. It's not a modern story. One of the hymns of the Rig Veda is spoken by a gambler, in his own voice, and it doesn't hold back.
screen: `HE PROMISED. HE MEANT IT.` → `THEN THE SOUND OF WINNING.` → `A GAMBLER'S HYMN.`

segments.voice: The gambler starts with the dice themselves. They thrill me, he says, in paraphrase, like a deep drink of soma. Then he tells what they cost. My wife never quarreled with me, never got angry. She was kind to me and to my friends. And for the sake of one losing throw, I drove away a devoted wife. Now his mother-in-law hates him. His wife pushes him away. His own family says, we don't know him, take him away. Other men court his wife while the dice take his wealth. And here's the line the hymn turns on. When I decide, I won't play with them, he says. I fall behind as my friends go off. But when the brown dice are thrown and their sound reaches me, off I go to the meeting place like a lover to a lover. His resolve doesn't fail from lack of knowing better. It fails at the sound. Meanwhile, the hymn says, the gambler's wife is left grieving, and his mother mourns a son wandering who knows where. Then a voice cuts through. Don't play with dice, it says. Farm your field. Be glad of what you have, and value it. There are your cattle, there is your wife. So says Savitar, the god who rouses, linked with the sun. The hymn doesn't end at the gaming table. It ends with a field, some cattle, and a wife at home.
screen: `THE DICE THRILL HIM LIKE SOMA.` · `HE DROVE AWAY A DEVOTED WIFE.` · `RESOLVE FAILS AT THE SOUND.` · `DON'T PLAY. FARM YOUR FIELD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your sound of the dice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of one pull in your life that gets past your good intentions: a phone, a snack, a game, an old argument you keep picking up. Don't scold yourself. Just notice what the trigger is. A sound, a time of day, a feeling. Then picture your field, the plain good things already in front of you: the people, the work, the home. Rest your attention there. If you pray, you can ask for strength in your own words. The bell holds the time.
What the Rig Veda is. Hymns of fire, dawn and the one called by many names, and also a gambler's confession, ending with Savitar's advice: farm your field. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT THE RIG VEDA IS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what the Rig Veda is. Today, when your own sound of the dice goes off, take one breath and look at your field instead. Tomorrow, a hymn that asks how everything began. Day one thousand two hundred forty-nine.

screen: `DAY 1249 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE NASADIYA SUKTA (THE HYMN OF CREATION — "WHO REALLY KNOWS?").`

howItsDone: The gambler's hymn is part of the Rig Veda's recited text, and Hindu teachers sometimes point to Savitar's advice in it, to leave the dice and tend one's field, as Vedic counsel against ruinous habits.

the dice thrill him, but the hymn tells what they cost and ends with Savitar saying: don't play.

he decides not to play, then the sound of the dice draws him back.

fork.setup: you're the gambler. you've promised yourself you're done. then you hear the brown dice thrown. what does the hymn say happens?
options: he goes to the meeting place like a lover.
he calls his wife for help.
fork.reveal: he says when he decides not to play, he falls behind his friends, but at the sound of the dice off he goes, like a lover to a lover.

original.note: Sanskrit: a die, one of the dice. The gambler's hymn is sometimes called the akṣa sukta, the hymn of the dice.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Rig Veda is only about gods and rituals.
what it means: it also keeps a gambler's confession, in his own voice, about what the dice cost him.
what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 10.34, the dice hymn, where resolve breaks at the sound of the dice and Savitar's counsel closes it: farm your field, there are your cattle, there your wife.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.34.1–5 (the dice delight like soma; a kind wife driven away for one throw; mother-in-law hates, family disowns; when I resolve not to play, the sound of the brown dice draws me back like a lover)
Rig Veda 10.34.10, 10.34.13 (the gambler's wife forlorn, his mother grieving; play not with dice, till your field, there are your cattle, there your wife: so says Savitar)

notes: Rig Veda 10.34 paraphrased (no PD translation on the validator list). Confirm verse numbers and that 'other men court his wife' (10.34.4) is fairly paraphrased.
The hook's casino scene is modern; the hymn's dice were nuts (vibhidaka), not mentioned here.
Original aksha (अक्ष) and 'akṣa sukta' as a name; confirm.
Savitar glossed as 'the god who rouses, linked with the sun'. Confirm the gloss.
Editor: replaced the 'not only... but' close repeated from 1247–1248 with a concrete ending from 10.34.13.
